81830.subject: 🪤Your Claude Code extension was fake
81830.body:
The Atlas

Автор: GenAI Works


Автор: GenAI Works

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/your-claude-code-extension-fake-genai-works-tcesf?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3B%2F1%2BSBZchR1S%2FyHgzqGDtLQ%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=10DHnc-JSz9sw1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~mvzfev2c~8m-null-null&eid=fz96fz-mvzfev2c-8m
  
Welcome back! A coding extension spent 11 hours handing out SSH backdoors, Musk admitted his agent loses money on every user, and Karpathy got tired of his YouTube feed and replaced it before lunch. In today's Atlas Newsletter: Somebody put a backdoor in Claude Code: Two tampered versions sat in Cursor’s marketplace, and separate malware is now sending stolen credentials to Claude for appraisal. Musk says Grok Bot costs too much: 800,000 paying users a week, and the CEO saying out loud that serving them doesn’t pay. Karpathy rebuilt YouTube in two hours: Every comment on Hacker News, sorted by Claude, turned into a feed built from human recommendations. Your model has a favorite random number: Across 18 model families, the chat versions were more predictable than the base ones every single time. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Somebody put a backdoor in Claude Code For about 11 hours on October 29, the Claude Code extension in Cursor’s marketplace was not the Claude Code extension. Two versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, had been tampered with.  Install one and it tries to set up a persistent SSH backdoor and collect information about your machine. Up to 5,000 developers may have pulled it down. Cursor removed the packages and posted instructions for cleaning up.  Anthropic says its own systems were never touched and that it neither wrote nor published the malicious code. Think about what a coding extension has access to.  Your source code. Your local files.  Whatever credentials you have sitting on that machine. That’s a better target than most companies. The same week, researchers found malware going the other way.  Volta-Autodoxer steals passwords, cards and logins off a machine, then sends the whole pile to Claude and asks it to build a profile of the victim and estimate what their accounts are worth. One attack aims at the AI tool. The other hires it. Our take: If you use Cursor, check whether either of those two versions landed on your machine and follow their guidance.  Then treat extension marketplaces the way you treat app stores, which is to say with a little suspicion.
